nameStory: The name 'nigra' comes from Latin meaning 'black,' referring to this spider's dark coloration. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, it belongs to the comb-footed spider family, named for the row of curved bristles on their back legs that look like tiny combs. These bristles help them handle their sticky silk when building their characteristic tangled webs.
description: Dipoena nigra is a small, dark comb-footed spider that builds irregular cobwebs in sheltered spots. Like other members of its family, it has a rounded abdomen and relatively long, thin legs compared to its body size. This is a tiny spider, with females typically measuring just a few millimeters in body length. Its dark coloration and small size make it easy to overlook, but its messy web often gives away its presence.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, rounded abdomen with a distinctly narrow waist connecting to the front body section, giving it the classic comb-footed spider silhouette

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Overall dark coloration ranging from deep brown to nearly black, with little to no visible patterning on the smooth abdomen

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates messy, three-dimensional cobwebs with sticky catching threads that feel tacky when accidentally walked through

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small spider, easily fitting on a fingernail with room to spare, often requiring close inspection to see details

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Usually hangs upside down in its web or retreats quickly to web edges when disturbed, moving with jerky, stop-and-go motions

habitat: Found in protected microhabitats like under loose tree bark, in rock crevices, or tucked into corners of human-made structures. Prefers spots that stay relatively dry but have enough moisture to prevent desiccation. Often discovered in leaf litter piles or among fallen logs in mixed forests throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to establish new webs in sheltered locations. Mating likely occurs during late spring months.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily found in their webs. Females may be carrying or guarding small, round egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active into early fall, with new generations emerging. Some individuals may begin seeking overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as juveniles or adults in protected locations under bark or deep in leaf litter, becoming dormant during coldest months.

funFact: Despite being incredibly small and seemingly fragile, comb-footed spiders like Dipoena nigra can capture prey much larger than themselves by using their sticky silk like a lasso, throwing it over insects that walk below their webs.
confusionNotes: Its small size and dark coloration make it easily confused with other tiny dark spiders, but the characteristic messy cobweb and rounded abdomen help distinguish it from sheet web spiders or jumping spiders of similar size.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Dipoena can be tricky to pronounce - it's 'die-POE-nah.' This spider is so small and inconspicuous that it's likely much more common than the few recorded observations suggest, simply because most people never notice it.
compareHints: Since no other Dipoena species are recorded in the New England dataset, compare it to other small, dark comb-footed spiders in the Theridiidae family. Unlike the more colorful or distinctly marked species in this family, Dipoena nigra lacks the bright reds, yellows, or clear patterns seen in relatives like the black widow or house spiders. Its uniform dark coloration and extremely small size set it apart from most other comb-footed spiders in the region.
